blocks.text: **Neutropenia** is a neutrophil count below about **1.5 × 10⁹/L**; the normal range shifts with age and ethnicity. Below **0.5 × 10⁹/L** the count is regarded as **critically low (severe)** and the risk of life-threatening bacterial infection climbs steeply.

blocks.title: How neutropenic fever is defined
rows: < 0.5 × 10⁹/L, **or < 1.0 × 10⁹/L if the nadir is expected to drop below 0.5 within 24 h**
One axillary reading > 38.5°C, **or three readings > 38.0°C within 12 h**
One oral reading ≥ 38.3°C (101°F), or ≥ 38.0°C (100.4°F) for ≥ 1 h
ANC < 500/µL, or < 1000/µL with a predicted nadir < 500/µL

blocks.title: Why it is an emergency
items: Left untreated it progresses to **sepsis with a high mortality** — it is an oncological emergency.
It is the **commonest reason a cancer patient comes to the emergency department**; think of it in **anyone unwell within a month of chemotherapy**.
Kumar & Clark Essentials: suspect neutropenic sepsis when neutrophils are < 1 × 10⁹/L and the patient has fever **or** new confusion, tachycardia, hypotension, breathlessness or hypothermia.

blocks.text: **ANC = total white cell count × % neutrophils** (segmented forms plus bands). A normal total WCC can hide a dangerously low ANC — always read the differential.

The books use **different temperature rules**. Davidson (oncology) wants ≥ 38°C for over an hour; Davidson (infectious disease) accepts one axillary reading > 38.5°C or three > 38.0°C in 12 h; the US (NCCN) rule accepts a **single oral 38.3°C**. Also remember the **"expected nadir" rule**: a count of 0.8 × 10⁹/L still qualifies if it is expected to fall below 0.5 × 10⁹/L within 24 h.

In cancer patients neutropenia is **usually caused by chemotherapy**. It can also follow **radiotherapy to large volumes of marrow**, or be part of a **pancytopenia from malignant marrow infiltration**. After chemotherapy the count bottoms out (the **nadir**) at roughly **7–10 days**, which is when fever typically appears.

blocks.title: Causes of neutropenia in general
rows: Viral; bacterial (e.g. _Salmonella_, overwhelming sepsis); protozoal (e.g. malaria)
Cytotoxic chemotherapy; idiosyncratic reactions (see list below) — **isolated agranulocytosis is usually drug-induced**
Leukaemia, lymphoma, myelodysplasia, metastatic cancer, aplastic anaemia, B12/folate deficiency
Connective tissue disease (e.g. SLE), hypersplenism, **Felty syndrome** (rheumatoid arthritis + splenomegaly + neutropenia), AIDS
Alcohol; congenital (**Kostmann syndrome**); constitutional (benign ethnic) neutropenia in people of African, Afro-Caribbean or Middle Eastern descent

blocks.title: Drugs that can cause neutropenia (Davidson Box 23.10)
items: Antithyroid: **carbimazole, propylthiouracil**
Anticonvulsants: phenytoin, sodium valproate, carbamazepine
Antibiotics: sulphonamides, penicillins, cephalosporins
Cardiovascular: captopril, enalapril, nifedipine; procainamide, quinidine
Others: gold, penicillamine; amitriptyline, mianserin; dapsone; cimetidine; zidovudine

blocks.title: Organisms in neutropenic fever
rows: Skin flora entering via cannulae and central lines
Gut flora crossing chemotherapy-damaged mucosa; cause **rapid deterioration**

blocks.text: Davidson says **Gram-positives are the commonest pathogens** (line-related). Pocket Medicine describes the classic mechanism as gut flora, especially Gram-negative rods such as _Pseudomonas_, seeding the blood, but notes that Gram-positives now account for 60–70% of the organisms identified. Reconcile them: Gram-positives are most frequent, but **Gram-negatives kill fastest**, so every empirical regimen must cover _Pseudomonas_.

Neutrophils are the front-line defence against bacteria and fungi. Without them, a bacteraemia is not contained and the patient can become **septicaemic and shocked within hours** unless antibiotics start immediately. The risk of sepsis depends on **how deep and how long** the neutropenia is, plus extra risk factors such as **IV cannulae and urinary catheters**.

blocks.title: Several defences fail at once in a cancer patient
items: **Chemotherapy** — fewer and poorly functioning neutrophils; myelosuppression is **dose-related**, and intensive curative regimens accept a small risk of fatal infection
**Mucositis** — the damaged gut lining lets **Gram-negative bowel organisms** into the blood
**Central lines and cannulae** — breach the skin and admit **staphylococci**
**The malignancy itself** — T- and B-cell defects
**Glucocorticoids** — impaired T-cell function and phagocytosis
**Obstruction** — of lymphatics, biliary tree, bowel or urinary tract

blocks.title: Typical infection patterns
items: Transient bacteraemia from **gut bacterial translocation**, cellulitis and pneumonia are the commonest infections
Most infections arise from the patient’s own **enteric flora** — the rationale for a low-contamination neutropenic diet
**Prolonged neutropenia plus antibiotic exposure** selects for fungal superinfection

blocks.text: Think of **two portals of entry**: the **gut** (mucositis → Gram-negatives such as _E. coli_ and _Pseudomonas_) and the **skin** (lines → _Staph. aureus_ and _Staph. epidermidis_).

Patients usually present with **high fever** and feel **non-specifically unwell**; examination rarely finds the source. **Fever is the first and often the only sign** of infection. There may be a sore throat, perianal pain or skin inflammation, and non-specific symptoms such as nausea, diarrhoea, drowsiness or breathlessness. **Tachycardia, hypotension or oliguria** mean systemic illness and need urgent admission and resuscitation.

**Fever may be absent.** Elderly patients and those on **antipyretics or glucocorticoids** may not mount a fever; **hypothermia or simple clinical deterioration** can be the first sign. Kumar & Clark: treat any fever after chemotherapy as possible neutropenic sepsis.

With no neutrophils the inflammatory response is weak, so **signs are blunted**: little neck stiffness in meningitis, a near-normal chest X-ray in pneumonia, no leucocytosis. **No neutrophils on a Gram stain does not exclude infection.**

blocks.title: Focused examination
items: Skin, including the **nail folds**; disseminated infection may show as skin lesions
Mouth and oropharynx (thrush, erythema, ulcers), sinuses and ears
Chest
**Central line, cannula and surgical wound sites**
Perianal area — **inspect only**
Abdomen — right lower quadrant pain suggests typhlitis

blocks.text: **Avoid digital rectal examination** in neutropenic patients, along with rectal thermometers, enemas and suppositories (risk of bacteraemia and bleeding).
Chronic or autoimmune neutropenia behaves differently: **recurrent sinusitis, stomatitis, gingivitis and perirectal infections** rather than acute sepsis.
The **full blood count with differential** is the critical test. Take the infection screen, then **start antibiotics without waiting for results**.

blocks.title: Initial work-up
rows: From a **peripheral vein and through each lumen of any central line**
Urine; sputum; stool if diarrhoea (including _C. difficile_); throat, line-site and wound swabs
FBC and differential, CRP, urea, creatinine and electrolytes, liver tests, clotting
**Chest X-ray for everyone**; chest CT if respiratory symptoms; abdominal imaging for right lower quadrant pain; sinus or CNS CT if localising features
Serum **galactomannan** and _Aspergillus_ PCR; **(1,3)-β-D-glucan** (does **not** detect mucoraceous moulds); cryptococcal antigen; CMV PCR; bronchoalveolar lavage for _Pneumocystis jirovecii_
Urine output, Glasgow Coma Scale, central venous pressure

blocks.text: **Cultures are often negative.** Adjust antibiotics if they grow something; if fever persists, look for an **occult source or abscess with CT**.

blocks.title: Features that predict lower risk
items: Onset as an outpatient, ECOG 0–1, age < 60, **solid tumour**, no symptoms, no major comorbidity, no previous fungal infection
**MASCC risk index ≥ 21**
Temperature < 39°C; no tachypnoea, hypotension, confusion or dehydration
Kumar & Clark: **no tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia or mucositis**, and myelosuppression expected to be **short**

blocks.note: Look at: panel A (neutrophil) beside the other white cells in panels B–E; Box 23.9 alongside lists the causes of neutropenia.

blocks.title: What goes wrong
items: **Septic shock and multi-organ failure** — **hypotension is an adverse prognostic sign** that can progress to circulatory collapse
Death — untreated neutropenic sepsis has a **high mortality**
**Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis)** — inflammation of the caecum: right lower quadrant pain, watery or bloody diarrhoea, caecal wall thickening on imaging
**Invasive fungal infection** (_Candida_, _Aspergillus_) — after prolonged neutropenia and antibiotics; suspect when fever persists
**_Pneumocystis jirovecii_ pneumonia** — a particular risk in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, hence co-trimoxazole prophylaxis during chemotherapy
Treatment toxicity — **amphotericin B deoxycholate is nephrotoxic**; lipid formulations are much less toxic

blocks.text: In aplastic anaemia, neutrophils < 0.5 × 10⁹/L (with platelets < 20 × 10⁹/L and reticulocytes < 40 × 10⁹/L) mark a **poor prognosis**; patients die of **infection or haemorrhage**.
Right lower quadrant pain in a neutropenic patient is **not automatically appendicitis** — think **typhlitis** and image the abdomen.

Treat as an **emergency**: take cultures, then give **broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour** of arrival (Kumar & Clark: hospitals need protocols for this). Choose according to **local policy and resistance patterns**, and discuss every case with the oncology team and microbiology.

blocks.title: Supportive care
items: IV fluid resuscitation, monitoring urine output, GCS and CVP
Early critical-care referral; inotropes, ventilation or haemofiltration if needed
Broaden Gram-negative and add Gram-positive cover if the patient deteriorates or stays febrile

blocks.title: Empirical antibiotics
rows: **Metronidazole** if anaerobes suspected; **teicoplanin** if Gram-positive infection suspected (e.g. central line)
IV piperacillin–tazobactam is the commonest regimen
Routine aminoglycoside **not** supported by trial data
Gentamicin + piperacillin–tazobactam, or meropenem alone (must cover _E. coli_, _Pseudomonas_, _Klebsiella_)
Vancomycin or teicoplanin for Gram-positive infection
Ceftazidime or piperacillin–tazobactam with gentamicin, or meropenem alone
Vancomycin for staphylococci, especially with lines
Antipseudomonal monotherapy: cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam, a carbapenem or ceftazidime
Vancomycin only for hypotension, pneumonia, line or soft-tissue infection, Gram-positive blood cultures, or mucositis on quinolone prophylaxis

blocks.text: **Gentamicin:** Davidson’s oncology and leukaemia sections list it as an option, but the infectious disease chapter says **routinely adding an aminoglycoside is not supported by trials**. In an MCQ, monotherapy with piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem is the safe first-line answer.

blocks.title: If the fever does not settle
items: At **36–48 h** without response: review antibiotics with microbiology and **consider antifungal cover** (Davidson, oncology)
Fever persisting **3–5 days**: add **empirical antifungal** — caspofungin, liposomal amphotericin B or voriconazole (Davidson)
**Pre-emptive** alternative: azole prophylaxis in high-risk patients, treating only when galactomannan or fungal PCR turns positive

Kumar & Clark’s opportunist cover: liposomal amphotericin B or voriconazole (_Candida_, _Aspergillus_); **high-dose co-trimoxazole** (_Pneumocystis_); **clarithromycin** (_Mycoplasma_, _Legionella_); anti-TB therapy
Lipid (liposomal) amphotericin B is used because it is **far less nephrotoxic** than amphotericin B deoxycholate

blocks.text: **Antifungal timing differs between books**: Davidson 3–5 days (with review at 36–48 h), First Aid 72 h, Pocket Medicine ≥ 4 days, Step-Up 4–7 days. Davidson’s 3–5 days is the reference answer.

blocks.title: Low-risk patients and duration
items: Selected **low-risk** patients (see risk features) can avoid or shorten admission with **oral co-amoxiclav plus ciprofloxacin**; avoid a quinolone regimen if already on quinolone prophylaxis
Known source: a full standard course (e.g. 14 days for bacteraemia)
No source found: continue until **afebrile and neutrophils > 0.5 × 10⁹/L** (Pocket Medicine); Kumar & Clark Essentials switches to oral after 48 h apyrexial, 10–14 days in total

blocks.text: **G-CSF is not given routinely** to every neutropenic patient, nor routinely in established neutropenic fever; its use follows guidelines (Davidson, First Aid). Step-Up’s “consider G-CSF” for persistent fever is the minority view.

blocks.title: Prevention
items: **Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis** (e.g. ciprofloxacin) in intermediate- or high-risk patients — reduces mortality

**Primary G-CSF prophylaxis** when the regimen’s febrile neutropenia risk is **> 20%** or the patient is high-risk (age, comorbidity); **secondary** after a previous episode; not in AML; it lowers febrile neutropenia rates but has **not been shown to reduce mortality**
Antifungal (posaconazole, fluconazole, micafungin) and antiviral (aciclovir, valaciclovir) prophylaxis in blood cancers; **co-trimoxazole** against _Pneumocystis_ in ALL

**Neutropenic diet**: avoid raw vegetables, unpeeled fruit, raw or rare meat, fish, undercooked eggs, salad-bar and deli food, soft blue-mould cheeses and well water; cooked, canned and pasteurised food is safe
Neutropenic precautions: hand hygiene, HEPA-filtered room, no plants or fresh flowers, no rectal procedures

blocks.alt: Algorithm: fever or unwell within a month of chemotherapy, then FBC and cultures, then IV antibiotics within 1 hour, review at 36–48 hours, and add an antifungal if fever persists for 3–5 days.

cards.back: Temperature ≥ 38°C for **more than 1 hour** with neutrophils **< 0.5 × 10⁹/L**, or < 1.0 × 10⁹/L if expected to fall below 0.5 within 24 h

cards.front: Davidson (infectious disease) temperature rule for neutropenic fever?
cards.back: One **axillary** reading > 38.5°C, or **three** readings > 38.0°C within 12 hours (with neutrophils < 0.5 × 10⁹/L)

cards.front: NCCN fever criterion used by US texts?
cards.back: A single oral temperature ≥ 38.3°C (101°F), or ≥ 38.0°C (100.4°F) sustained for ≥ 1 hour

cards.front: Commonest cause of neutropenia in a cancer patient, and when does fever usually occur?
cards.back: **Chemotherapy**; at the nadir, about **7–10 days** after treatment
**Gram-positive cocci** (_Staph. aureus_, _Staph. epidermidis_), especially with indwelling lines

cards.front: Two antithyroid drugs that can cause neutropenia?
How do gut Gram-negatives reach the blood after chemotherapy?
cards.back: Chemotherapy-induced **mucositis** breaks the gut mucosal barrier

cards.front: What determines the risk of sepsis in a neutropenic patient?
cards.back: The **severity and duration** of neutropenia, plus extra risk factors such as IV cannulae and urinary catheters

cards.front: Who may have neutropenic sepsis without a fever?
cards.back: The elderly and patients on **antipyretics or glucocorticoids**; hypothermia or deterioration may be the first sign

cards.front: Which examination should be avoided in a neutropenic patient?
cards.back: **Digital rectal examination** (inspect the perianal area only)

cards.front: Where should blood cultures be taken from?
cards.back: A **peripheral vein and every lumen of any central line**

cards.front: Which fungal marker misses mucoraceous moulds?
cards.back: (1,3)-β-D-glucan; galactomannan and _Aspergillus_ PCR are used for aspergillosis
Right lower quadrant pain, watery or bloody diarrhoea, **caecal wall thickening** on imaging
**Hypotension** — may progress to circulatory collapse and multi-organ failure

cards.front: Target time to first antibiotic dose?
cards.back: **Within 1 hour** of arrival in the emergency department
**Piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem** monotherapy (± gentamicin per local policy); add metronidazole for anaerobes, teicoplanin for Gram-positives/lines

cards.front: When is an empirical antifungal added (Davidson)?
cards.back: If fever persists **3–5 days** despite antibiotics (review at 36–48 h): e.g. caspofungin, liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole

cards.front: Oral regimen for selected low-risk patients?

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman is 9 days into a cycle of docetaxel for breast cancer. Her temperature is 38.1°C at 14:00 and 38.2°C at 15:20. Her neutrophil count is 0.4 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: Using Davidson’s oncology definition, which combination makes this neutropenic fever?
options: Temperature ≥ 37.5°C on one reading with neutrophils < 1.5 × 10⁹/L
Temperature > 39°C on one reading with neutrophils < 2.0 × 10⁹/L
Temperature ≥ 38°C for over 24 hours with neutrophils < 0.1 × 10⁹/L
Temperature ≥ 38°C for over 1 hour with neutrophils < 0.5 × 10⁹/L
Temperature ≥ 38°C for over 1 hour with lymphocytes < 1.0 × 10⁹/L
questions.explanation: Davidson defines neutropenic fever as **≥ 38°C lasting more than 1 hour** with neutrophils **< 0.5 × 10⁹/L** (or < 1.0 if expected to fall below 0.5 within 24 h). She has been above 38°C for over an hour with a count of 0.4.
whyNot: 37.5°C is not a threshold, and < 1.5 × 10⁹/L defines neutropenia, not the febrile-neutropenia count.
No book requires 39°C, and 2.0 × 10⁹/L is not neutropenic.
Waiting 24 hours would be dangerous; the duration needed is 1 hour and the count is < 0.5.
The definition uses neutrophils, not lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with lymphoma is 6 days after chemotherapy. His temperature has been 38.2°C for 2 hours. His neutrophil count is 0.8 × 10⁹/L, and the haematology team expect it to drop below 0.5 × 10⁹/L within the next day.
questions.leadIn: How should this episode be classified?
options: Not neutropenic fever, because the count is above 0.5 × 10⁹/L
Not neutropenic fever, because the temperature is below 38.5°C
Neutropenic fever only once a source of infection is found
Neutropenic fever only if the count stays low for over 7 days
Neutropenic fever, to be treated as an emergency
questions.explanation: Davidson’s definition includes a count **< 1.0 × 10⁹/L when the nadir is expected to fall below 0.5 × 10⁹/L within 24 hours**. With a sustained temperature ≥ 38°C, this is neutropenic fever and needs immediate antibiotics.
whyNot: The "expected nadir" rule extends the definition to counts below 1.0 × 10⁹/L that are expected to fall below 0.5 × 10⁹/L within 24 hours.
38.5°C is only one alternative (single axillary reading); ≥ 38°C for over 1 hour also qualifies.
A source is rarely found; treatment must not wait for one.
Duration of neutropenia affects risk, not whether the episode is defined as neutropenic fever.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with acute myeloid leukaemia has a tunnelled central venous catheter. On day 11 of induction chemotherapy he develops a fever of 38.6°C. The skin around the exit site is red, and blood cultures drawn through the line grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
questions.leadIn: Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Gram-positive skin organisms — _Staph. aureus_ and _Staph. epidermidis_ — are the commonest cause of severe neutropenic sepsis and enter **via cannulae and central lines**. Gram-positive cocci in clusters from a line fits staphylococci.
whyNot: A Gram-negative rod from the gut; it would not appear as Gram-positive cocci.
A Gram-negative rod that enters through damaged gut mucosa.
A mould; it does not grow as cocci in blood cultures and causes later, persistent fever.
A yeast; it is not a Gram-positive coccus in clusters.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with Graves’ disease presents with a sore throat and a temperature of 38.8°C. Her neutrophil count is 0.2 × 10⁹/L; haemoglobin and platelets are normal. Her medicines are carbimazole (started 6 weeks ago), propranolol, a combined oral contraceptive, omeprazole and occasional paracetamol.
questions.leadIn: Which medicine is most likely to have caused her neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Antithyroid drugs (**carbimazole, propylthiouracil**) are classic causes of drug-induced neutropenia; an isolated agranulocytosis is usually a drug reaction. Sore throat with fever is a typical presentation.
whyNot: Beta-blockers are not on the list of drugs that cause neutropenia.
Oral contraceptives are not a recognised cause.
Omeprazole is not listed; the H₂ blocker cimetidine is.
Paracetamol is not a recognised cause of agranulocytosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is 10 days after chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He has painful mouth ulcers and diarrhoea, and a fever of 38.7°C. He has no central line. Blood cultures grow _Escherichia coli_.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains how this organism entered his bloodstream?
options: Contamination of an IV cannula by skin flora
Chemotherapy-induced mucositis breaching the gut lining
Aspiration of oral secretions into the lungs
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy damages rapidly dividing mucosa. **Mucositis** opens the gut barrier, so **Gram-negative bowel organisms** such as _E. coli_ enter the blood. His mouth ulcers and diarrhoea show the mucosal damage.
whyNot: Skin flora via cannulae are typically staphylococci, not _E. coli_.
Steroids impair T cells and phagocytosis but do not explain a gut organism entering the blood.
Hypersplenism is a cause of neutropenia, not a portal of entry.
Aspiration causes pneumonia; _E. coli_ bacteraemia with gut symptoms points to the bowel.

questions.stem: Two patients with breast cancer develop neutropenia after the same chemotherapy regimen. One has a neutrophil count of 0.1 × 10⁹/L expected to last 10 days and a urinary catheter; the other has 0.9 × 10⁹/L expected to recover in 2 days.
questions.leadIn: Which factor best explains why the first patient has the higher risk of sepsis?
options: Her greater depth and duration of neutropenia, plus a catheter
The histological grade of her tumour
The time of day the chemotherapy was given
questions.explanation: Sepsis risk relates to the **severity and duration of neutropenia** and to added risk factors such as **IV cannulae and bladder catheters**.
whyNot: Anaemia does not determine bacterial infection risk here.
Platelets affect bleeding risk, not infection risk.
Tumour grade does not directly set the infection risk of neutropenia.
Timing of administration is irrelevant.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is 8 days after carboplatin for lung cancer and is taking dexamethasone. His daughter says he has become confused today. Temperature 35.6°C, pulse 114/min, BP 92/58 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Rewarm him and recheck the temperature in 4 hours before deciding
Take blood cultures and give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour
Stop dexamethasone and observe for steroid-induced delirium
Arrange a CT head before starting any treatment
Wait for blood culture results before choosing an antibiotic
questions.explanation: Fever may be **absent** in elderly patients and those on **steroids**; **hypothermia or clinical deterioration** can be the first sign. Tachycardia and hypotension after recent chemotherapy mean presumed neutropenic sepsis: cultures, then IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
whyNot: Delaying for a fever wastes the critical first hour; hypothermia can itself signal sepsis.
Steroids may mask fever; stopping them does not treat the likely sepsis.
Imaging must not delay antibiotics in a hypotensive post-chemotherapy patient.
Cultures are often negative; antibiotics are started without waiting.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia has a fever of 38.4°C and complains of perianal pain. Her neutrophil count is 0.1 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: Which part of the examination should be avoided?
options: Inspection of the central line exit site
Inspection of the finger and toe nail folds
questions.explanation: In neutropenic patients **digital rectal examination is avoided**; the perianal area is inspected instead. Rectal thermometers, enemas and suppositories are also avoided.
whyNot: Inspecting the perianal area is recommended.
Line sites are a key source and must be examined.
The mouth and pharynx should be checked for thrush and ulcers.
Davidson specifically advises close inspection around the nails.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a PICC line is admitted with neutropenic fever 8 days after chemotherapy for breast cancer.
questions.leadIn: Which blood culture strategy is most appropriate?
options: A peripheral sample plus a sample from each lumen of the line
A sample from the line only
A peripheral sample only, after removing the line
A single sample once the temperature exceeds 39°C
A single sample after the first antibiotic dose
questions.explanation: Cultures should be taken from **both a peripheral vein and the central line** (each lumen), then antibiotics started without waiting for results.
whyNot: A line-only sample cannot separate line colonisation from bacteraemia.
The line is not removed routinely before culturing.
There is no 39°C threshold; delaying cultures delays antibiotics.
Cultures should be taken before antibiotics to maximise yield.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a germ-cell tumour develops a fever of 38.4°C at home 9 days after chemotherapy. He has no significant comorbidities. On examination he has painful oral mucositis; pulse 88/min, BP 126/78 mmHg, SpO₂ 98%.
questions.leadIn: Which feature argues most strongly against managing him as low risk with oral antibiotics?
questions.explanation: Kumar & Clark’s low-risk criteria require **no tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia or mucositis** and a short expected neutropenia. Mucositis also means poor oral absorption and a breached gut barrier.
whyNot: Age < 60 is a lower-risk feature.
A solid tumour is a lower-risk feature.
Outpatient onset is a lower-risk feature.
A temperature below 39°C is a lower-risk feature.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is 12 days into induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia. He has right lower quadrant pain, watery diarrhoea streaked with blood and a fever of 38.9°C. Neutrophils are 0.1 × 10⁹/L. CT shows thickening of the caecal wall.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Typhlitis** is inflammation of the caecum specific to neutropenia: right lower quadrant pain, watery or bloody diarrhoea and **caecal wall thickening**.
whyNot: Appendicitis is possible, but profound neutropenia plus caecal wall thickening points to typhlitis.
_C. difficile_ causes diffuse colitis; localised caecal thickening in neutropenia suggests typhlitis.
Ischaemic colitis affects older patients and watershed areas, not the caecum in neutropenia.
A new presentation during induction chemotherapy with caecal thickening is not typical of Crohn’s disease.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia develops a dry cough, fever and hypoxia. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows _Pneumocystis jirovecii_.
questions.leadIn: Which prophylactic agent is given during ALL chemotherapy to prevent this infection?
questions.explanation: Patients with ALL are prone to **_Pneumocystis_ pneumonia**, so **co-trimoxazole prophylaxis** is given throughout chemotherapy; treatment is with high-dose co-trimoxazole.
whyNot: Fluconazole prevents _Candida_, not _Pneumocystis_.
Aciclovir prevents herpesvirus reactivation.
Ciprofloxacin is antibacterial prophylaxis.
Itraconazole is used against _Aspergillus_, not _Pneumocystis_.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with colon cancer is admitted 10 days after chemotherapy with a temperature of 38.6°C for 2 hours and neutrophils of 0.3 × 10⁹/L. Pulse 104/min, BP 112/70 mmHg. He has no allergies.
questions.leadIn: Which empirical antibiotic is most appropriate as first line?
questions.explanation: Davidson’s first-line empirical therapy is **piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem**, giving broad cover including _Pseudomonas_ and enteric Gram-negatives, started IV within an hour.
whyNot: Oral amoxicillin lacks antipseudomonal cover and is too narrow for an admitted, tachycardic patient.
Vancomycin covers only Gram-positives; Gram-negatives must be covered from the start.
An antifungal is not first-line; it is added for persistent fever.
Clarithromycin covers atypical organisms only.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with neutropenic fever needs an empirical antifungal. The team chooses liposomal amphotericin B rather than conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate.
questions.leadIn: What is the main reason for this choice?
options: It is absorbed well by mouth
It does not need IV access
questions.explanation: Lipid formulations of amphotericin B have similar efficacy but **far fewer adverse effects**; amphotericin B deoxycholate commonly causes **nephrotoxicity**. Lipid forms are used as empirical therapy in neutropenic fever.
whyNot: Both forms are given intravenously.
Amphotericin has no antibacterial activity.
Cost is not the reason given; the lipid formulation is chosen because its adverse effects, including nephrotoxicity, are much less frequent.
It is an IV drug.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man of Afro-Caribbean descent has a neutrophil count of 1.2 × 10⁹/L on a routine pre-employment blood test. He is well, has had no recurrent infections, and his haemoglobin, platelets and blood film are otherwise normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Davidson lists **constitutional neutropenia** in people of Afro-Caribbean and Middle Eastern descent; the normal neutrophil range varies with ethnicity. A well man with a mild isolated low count fits.
whyNot: Kostmann syndrome is a congenital, severe neutropenia with infections from childhood.
Leukaemia would usually affect other lineages or show blasts.
Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia.
He takes no drugs, and agranulocytosis means a very low count.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman receives her first cycle of adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer.
questions.leadIn: When is neutropenic fever most likely to develop after this cycle?
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenic fever usually occurs at the **neutrophil nadir, about 7–10 days** after treatment.
whyNot: The count has not yet fallen in the first days.
By 3–4 weeks the count has usually recovered, ready for the next cycle.
This is well after the usual nadir.
Long after the nadir.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with myeloma has a neutrophil count of 0.3 × 10⁹/L. His axillary temperatures are 38.1°C at 08:00, 38.2°C at 13:00 and 38.1°C at 18:00. He feels well.
questions.leadIn: Under Davidson’s infectious disease definition, how should this be interpreted?
options: Not neutropenic fever, because no single reading exceeds 39°C
Not neutropenic fever, because he feels well
Not neutropenic fever, because the readings were 5 hours apart
Neutropenic fever only if CRP is raised
Neutropenic fever, because there are three readings above 38.0°C within 12 hours
questions.explanation: Davidson’s infectious disease chapter accepts **one axillary reading > 38.5°C or three readings > 38.0°C over 12 hours** with neutrophils < 0.5 × 10⁹/L.
whyNot: No definition requires 39°C.
Patients are often only non-specifically unwell; feeling well does not exclude it.
Three readings spread across 12 hours is exactly the criterion.
CRP is not part of the definition.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with neutropenic fever after chemotherapy for ovarian cancer deteriorates rapidly over a few hours with hypotension. Her mucositis is severe.
questions.leadIn: Which organism must the empirical regimen always cover from the outset?
questions.explanation: Gut-derived Gram-negatives (_E. coli_, _Klebsiella_, **_Pseudomonas_**) cause **rapid deterioration** and must be covered by the initial empirical regimen (hence piperacillin–tazobactam, meropenem or ceftazidime).
whyNot: Gram-positive or MRSA cover is added for specific indications such as line infection.
Antifungal cover is added for persistent fever, not from the outset.
Antifungals are added later if fever persists.
_Pneumocystis_ is covered by prophylaxis or treated when found, not by the initial empirical regimen.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with acute leukaemia has been on piperacillin–tazobactam for neutropenic fever for 24 hours. The skin around his Hickman line exit site is now red, tender and discharging pus.
questions.leadIn: Which addition to his treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Suspected **Gram-positive (line-related) infection** calls for **teicoplanin or vancomycin** on top of the antipseudomonal backbone.
whyNot: Metronidazole is added for suspected anaerobic infection.
Gentamicin broadens Gram-negative cover; it does not treat staphylococcal line infection well.
An antifungal is not indicated for an acute purulent exit-site infection.
Aciclovir treats herpesviruses.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor asks about granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) for a patient admitted with neutropenic fever.
questions.leadIn: Which statement is most accurate?
options: It should be given to every patient with neutropenia
It has been shown to reduce mortality in febrile neutropenia
It is not used routinely in established neutropenic fever; its use follows guidelines
It is the preferred primary prophylaxis in acute myeloid leukaemia
It can replace antibiotics in low-risk patients
questions.explanation: Davidson: **G-CSF is not used routinely** for all neutropenic patients; guidelines govern its use. First Aid agrees it is not routinely indicated in established neutropenic fever. Its main role is **primary prophylaxis** (regimen risk > 20%) or **secondary prophylaxis** after a previous episode.
whyNot: Routine use for all patients is explicitly not recommended.
It reduces febrile neutropenia rates but has not been shown to reduce mortality.
Colony-stimulating factors are not used in AML.
Nothing replaces prompt antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman remains febrile on day 5 of piperacillin–tazobactam for neutropenic fever after AML induction. CT chest shows nodules. The team wants a blood test for invasive aspergillosis.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: **Galactomannan** (and _Aspergillus_ PCR) detects _Aspergillus_ in blood; a positive result can trigger pre-emptive antifungal therapy.
whyNot: Cryptococcal antigen detects _Cryptococcus neoformans_.
CMV PCR detects cytomegalovirus.
Urinary antigen detects _Legionella pneumophila_ type 1.
ASO is for streptococcal infection and antibody tests are rarely useful in immunocompromised patients.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is being discharged between chemotherapy cycles and is given advice on a neutropenic diet.
questions.leadIn: Which food should he avoid?
questions.explanation: Kumar & Clark’s neutropenic diet avoids foods likely to carry bacteria or fungi, including **soft blue-mould cheeses**, raw vegetables, rare meat, fish, undercooked eggs, deli and salad-bar food.
whyNot: Canned fruit is listed as safe.
Well-done meat is safe.
Hard-boiled eggs with no runny yolk are safe.
Pasteurised dairy is safe.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with breast cancer is 8 days after her third cycle of chemotherapy. She has felt shivery for 2 hours. Temperature 38.4°C for 90 minutes, pulse 108/min, BP 100/64 mmHg. She has an implanted port. Neutrophils 0.2 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral co-amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin at home
Wait for blood culture results, then start a targeted antibiotic
Blood cultures from a peripheral vein and the port, then IV piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 hour
G-CSF injection and review in 24 hours
questions.explanation: **Step 1 — recognise it:** ≥ 38°C for over an hour with neutrophils < 0.5 × 10⁹/L is neutropenic fever (Davidson), an emergency. **Step 2 — assess risk:** tachycardia and borderline BP mean she is not low risk, so she needs admission and IV treatment. **Step 3 — investigate quickly:** cultures from a peripheral vein **and the port**, urine, CXR. **Step 4 — treat within the hour:** broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering _Pseudomonas_ — piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem — without waiting for results.
whyNot: Oral treatment is only for low-risk patients without tachycardia or hypotension.
Cultures are often negative and the delay can be fatal.
Vancomycin alone misses the Gram-negatives that cause rapid deterioration.
G-CSF is not routine in established neutropenic fever and does not replace antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a testicular germ-cell tumour phones the chemotherapy unit 9 days after treatment with a temperature of 38.3°C sustained for an hour. In clinic: pulse 84/min, BP 128/80 mmHg, SpO₂ 98% on air, no mouth ulcers. Neutrophils 0.4 × 10⁹/L, expected to recover within a few days. The unit has an established febrile neutropenia service.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management after cultures?
options: Oral co-amoxiclav plus ciprofloxacin with close follow-up
IV meropenem and vancomycin in intensive care
No antibiotics; repeat blood count in 48 hours
questions.explanation: **Step 1 — confirm:** he has neutropenic fever. **Step 2 — stratify:** solid tumour, outpatient onset, age < 60, no tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia or mucositis, short expected neutropenia → **low risk**. **Step 3 — choose:** in experienced units low-risk patients can avoid or shorten admission with **oral co-amoxiclav plus ciprofloxacin**. **Step 4 — safety-net:** he still needs cultures and close review; if he deteriorates, admit for IV therapy.
whyNot: Intensive care and dual IV therapy are excessive for a stable, low-risk patient.
Neutropenic fever always needs antibiotics.
An antifungal is not first-line.
Antifungals are reserved for persistent fever.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with AML has had neutropenic fever for 5 days. She has received piperacillin–tazobactam since admission and teicoplanin since day 2. Blood cultures are negative. She is still febrile at 38.8°C. CT chest shows several nodules, and serum galactomannan is positive.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop all antibiotics to allow a diagnostic window
Start G-CSF and continue the current regimen unchanged
Add an antifungal such as voriconazole or liposomal amphotericin B
Switch to oral co-amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin
questions.explanation: **Step 1 — note the time course:** fever persisting **3–5 days** despite broad-spectrum antibacterials is Davidson’s trigger for antifungal therapy (review starts at 36–48 h). **Step 2 — look for evidence:** CT nodules and a **positive galactomannan** point to invasive _Aspergillus_. **Step 3 — act:** add **liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole or caspofungin**. Lipid amphotericin is preferred over the deoxycholate form because it is less nephrotoxic.
whyNot: More Gram-negative cover will not treat a fungal infection.
Stopping treatment in persistent neutropenic fever is dangerous.
G-CSF is not routine and does nothing for the established fungal infection.
Oral step-down is for patients who are improving and low risk.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate antimicrobial to start or add. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with breast cancer, 9 days after chemotherapy, has a temperature of 38.2°C for 2 hours and neutrophils of 0.4 × 10⁹/L. She is well, with normal observations and no mucositis; recovery is expected within days. The unit runs a febrile neutropenia service.
items.explanation: Low-risk features (no tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia or mucositis; short neutropenia) allow **oral co-amoxiclav plus ciprofloxacin** in experienced units.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy on chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia stopped taking his prophylactic tablets. He now has fever, a dry cough and falling oxygen saturation; bronchoalveolar lavage identifies _Pneumocystis jirovecii_.
items.explanation: ALL with missed co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and _Pneumocystis_ on BAL → treat with **high-dose co-trimoxazole**.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man on piperacillin–tazobactam for neutropenic fever is still febrile on day 3. He now has a fluctuant, foul-smelling perianal collection, and the team suspects anaerobic infection.
items.explanation: Davidson: add **metronidazole** when anaerobic infection is suspected.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with lymphoma remains febrile despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. She has a new cough, diarrhoea and confusion; a urinary antigen test is positive for _Legionella pneumophila_ serogroup 1.
items.explanation: Two steps: positive urinary antigen → _Legionella_ → Kumar & Clark’s opportunist cover lists **clarithromycin** for _Mycoplasma_ and _Legionella_.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with AML on piperacillin–tazobactam develops redness, tenderness and pus at his tunnelled central line exit site; blood cultures from the line grow Gram-positive cocci.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with small cell lung cancer received carboplatin and etoposide 10 days ago. She presents with nausea, drowsiness and breathlessness. Temperature 36.9°C, pulse 112/min, BP 96/60 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most important to request first?
questions.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is the commonest reason a cancer patient attends the emergency department and must be considered in anyone unwell within a month of chemotherapy. Fever may be absent and symptoms non-specific; the **full blood count is the critical test**. Tachycardia and hypotension demand urgent resuscitation.
whyNot: Hypercalcaemia can cause drowsiness, but tachycardia and hypotension 10 days after chemotherapy make neutropenic sepsis the first thing to exclude.
Imaging is secondary and must not delay antibiotics.
There is no chest pain to suggest a coronary event.
PE is possible but the timing after chemotherapy makes neutropenic sepsis the priority.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has recurrent chest infections. Examination shows splenomegaly. Her neutrophil count is 0.9 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Felty syndrome** is the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly and neutropenia.
whyNot: Kostmann syndrome is congenital and presents in childhood.
Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia without splenomegaly.
SLE can cause neutropenia but does not fit long-standing RA with splenomegaly.
Constitutional neutropenia is benign and not linked with RA or splenomegaly.

questions.stem: A registrar is writing a neutropenic fever protocol for a stable patient with no line and no suspected focus. She asks whether gentamicin should routinely be added to IV piperacillin–tazobactam.
questions.leadIn: Which statement best reflects Davidson’s infectious disease chapter?
options: Gentamicin must always be added to cover _Pseudomonas_
Trial data do not support routinely adding an aminoglycoside
An aminoglycoside should be added only after 5 days of fever
Gentamicin is contraindicated in every neutropenic patient
questions.explanation: Davidson’s infectious disease chapter states that piperacillin–tazobactam IV is the commonest regimen and that **routinely adding an aminoglycoside is not supported by trial data**. The oncology chapter still allows gentamicin by local policy.
whyNot: Piperacillin–tazobactam already covers _Pseudomonas_.
Gentamicin alone is not a first-line regimen.
Persistent fever at 3–5 days prompts antifungal therapy, not an aminoglycoside.
It remains an option under local policy; it is not contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with AML is 13 days into induction chemotherapy. He has a fever of 38.7°C and new right lower quadrant pain and tenderness. Neutrophils are 0.1 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most appropriate next?
questions.explanation: Right lower quadrant pain in neutropenia raises **typhlitis**; Davidson recommends **abdominal imaging**, which shows caecal wall thickening.
whyNot: Endoscopy is invasive and not the first test in profound neutropenia.
Contrast enemas are not the investigation of choice and involve rectal instrumentation.
Rectal examination is avoided in neutropenic patients.
Surgery is not the first step; imaging comes first.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with lymphoma has been on IV antibiotics for neutropenic fever for 4 days. No source was found and cultures are negative. He has been afebrile for 24 hours, but his neutrophil count is still 0.2 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: According to Pocket Medicine, what is the most appropriate plan?
options: Stop antibiotics now that he is afebrile
Continue antibiotics until he is afebrile and neutrophils exceed 0.5 × 10⁹/L
Stop antibiotics once the CRP is normal, whatever the neutrophil count
questions.explanation: With **no source**, antibiotics continue until the patient is **afebrile and the ANC exceeds 500/µL** (0.5 × 10⁹/L). A known source gets a full standard course (e.g. 14 days for bacteraemia).
whyNot: He is still profoundly neutropenic; stopping risks relapse of sepsis.
CRP is not the stopping rule.
Six weeks is far longer than needed without a deep-seated source.
G-CSF is not a substitute for antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman on chemotherapy for ovarian cancer has neutrophils of 0.3 × 10⁹/L. Her first and only oral temperature reading is 38.4°C.
questions.leadIn: Under the NCCN definition used in US texts, how should this be interpreted?
options: Neutropenic fever, because a single oral reading ≥ 38.3°C qualifies
Not neutropenic fever until a second reading is taken 1 hour later
Not neutropenic fever until the temperature reaches 39°C
Not neutropenic fever, because the count is above 0.1 × 10⁹/L
Neutropenic fever only if blood cultures are positive
questions.explanation: NCCN (Pocket Medicine, First Aid): a **single oral temperature ≥ 38.3°C**, or ≥ 38.0°C sustained for ≥ 1 hour, with ANC < 500/µL. Davidson’s oncology definition instead needs ≥ 38°C for over an hour.
whyNot: The sustained-1-hour rule applies to readings of 38.0–38.2°C, not to 38.3°C or above.
No definition requires 39°C.
The threshold is < 0.5 × 10⁹/L (500/µL).
Cultures are often negative and are not part of the definition.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted with neutropenic fever 9 days after chemotherapy for bladder cancer. He has a temperature of 39.0°C, a sore throat, mild diarrhoea and neutrophils of 0.4 × 10⁹/L. His BP is 84/50 mmHg despite an initial fluid bolus.
questions.leadIn: Which finding carries the worst prognosis?
questions.explanation: Davidson: **hypotension is an adverse prognostic feature** and can progress to circulatory collapse and organ failure. It calls for resuscitation, early critical care and inotropes.
whyNot: High fever is typical and not in itself prognostic.
A sore throat is a common local symptom.
Non-specific gut symptoms are common.
The count defines the condition; hypotension marks the dangerous course.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia on steroid-containing induction is classed as high risk for neutropenic infection. The team considers antibacterial prophylaxis.
questions.leadIn: Which prophylaxis has been shown to reduce mortality in this setting?
questions.explanation: Pocket Medicine notes that **fluoroquinolone prophylaxis** in intermediate- or high-risk neutropenia (especially ALL on steroids) **reduces mortality**; Kumar & Clark also lists ciprofloxacin prophylaxis.
whyNot: G-CSF lowers febrile neutropenia rates but has not been shown to reduce mortality.
Oral vancomycin is for _C. difficile_, not prophylaxis.
Carbapenems are for treatment, not prophylaxis.
IVIG is used only rarely in neutropenia and has no shown mortality benefit as prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with lymphoma has neutropenic fever. He develops a cough and his oxygen saturation falls to 91% on air, but his chest X-ray is reported as normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Sputum Gram stain, treating only if neutrophils are seen
questions.explanation: Neutropenia blunts the inflammatory response, so the **chest X-ray may look normal** in pneumonia. Davidson advises **chest CT in addition to CXR** when there are respiratory symptoms; it can also reveal fungal nodules.
whyNot: Waiting a week risks missing a rapidly progressive infection.
Absence of neutrophils on Gram stain does not exclude infection in neutropenia.
Spirometry does not identify infection.
A V/Q scan looks for PE; infection must be looked for first in this setting.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with breast cancer has been on piperacillin–tazobactam for neutropenic fever for 48 hours. She remains febrile at 38.6°C, haemodynamically stable, and cultures are negative.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson’s oncology chapter, what should happen now?
options: Switch to oral co-amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin
Review antibiotics with microbiology advice and consider antifungal cover
Continue the same regimen unchanged for 14 days
questions.explanation: Davidson’s oncology chapter: when fever has **not responded by 36–48 hours**, the regimen is **reconsidered with the microbiologists** and **antifungal cover (liposomal amphotericin B) is considered**.
whyNot: Stopping in persistent neutropenic fever is dangerous.
Oral step-down is for low-risk or improving patients.
G-CSF is not routine.
A non-responding regimen should be reviewed, not left unchanged.
